newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani minister says official media not needed.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani minister says official media not needed.

text.p: Caretaker Information Minister Irshad Haqqani said on Saturday that Pakistan did not need an official news agency, and ations should be allowed to compete with their state-run counterparts.
"No news agency should be under the direct control of the government," Haqqani told Reuters in an interview. "In principle I think that this agency should be in the private sector."
But he said privatising Pakistan's official APP news agency was unlikely to take place under the caretaker government charged with supervising elections on February 3.

"I don't think it is possible in this government," he said, adding that the interim cabinet's priorities were holding the elections on time, starting an anti-corruption process and tackling Pakistan's severe economic problems.
Haqqani, a journalist by profession, said he also favoured liberalising television and radio, including news broadcasts.
"We should allow totally independent stations and channels. They should be free and the official electronic media should compete with them," he said. "Why this monopoly?"
Pakistan state radio and television enjoy a near-monopoly at present. A semi-independent television channel broadcasts mainly entertainment programmes, but may not carry its own news.
Haqqani said one obstacle to privatising APP was its large staff of about 500 employees, many of whom would have to be laid off if the agency was sold to the private sector.
He said the government was arranging televised panel discussions on current affairs, bringing together politicians from different parties, and was broadcasting them unedited.
"I want to give credibility to the electronic media controlled by the government," Haqqani said.
He said different political parties would be given air time ahead of the February 3 polls and limits set on campaign expenses, but said the details had not yet been worked out.

President Farooq Leghari appointed a caretaker government after dissolving the National Assembly (lower house) and sacking Benazir Bhutto's three-year-old government on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule.
